title: SYNTRA: An Entropy-Optimized, Mathematically Formalized Interlinguistic Protocol for M2M, LLM, and Human-Cognitive Architecture
abstract: SYNTRA: An Entropy-Optimized, Mathematically Formalized Interlinguistic Protocol for M2M, LLM, and Human-Cognitive Architecture Author: Yildiray Yildirim (2026)DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22860133Version: 1.1 ABSTRACT SYNTRA proposes an entropy-reduced semantic communication protocol designed to establish a mathematically formalized interlinguistic standard for machine-to-machine (M2M), large language model (LLM), and human-cognitive communication. By leveraging a deterministic LL(1) parsing model, the architecture is designed to eliminate syntactic ambiguity at the protocol layer and reduce ambiguity-related error pathways before semantic reasoning is performed. Rather than modifying the internal computational complexity of Transformer architectures, SYNTRA operates at the communication and representation layer, where deterministic parsing and semantic compression may reduce the effective sequence length presented to downstream LLMs. Operating strictly within the 95 printable ASCII characters (decimal range [32, 126]), the protocol defines a core vocabulary of 1,000 root lexemes and 15 deterministic morphological operators. Core primitives are represented using a 14-bit binary encoding structure, while complex nesting, typing, and structural serialization are resolved deterministically through a formal context-free grammar implemented by a Deterministic Pushdown Automaton (DPDA / Kellerautomat). Based on theoretical upper-bound projections and simulation assumptions, the architecture indicates a potential reduction in downstream LLM inference compute requirements of up to 64% under a specified 40% sequence-length reduction assumption. This follows from the quadratic attention relationship: (0.6N)^2 = 0.36N^2 Accordingly, the theoretical attention-compute component associated with the compressed sequence would represent approximately 36% of the corresponding uncompressed sequence length term. Macroeconomic implications, including projected energy savings of up to 89.6 TWh/year and infrastructure cost optimization, are presented strictly as model-based projections pending empirical validation at large scale. 1. INTRODUCTION & MOTIVATION Traditional natural-language interfaces for Large Language Models and distributed AI systems introduce substantial linguistic redundancy, contextual ambiguity, and variable tokenization overhead. SYNTRA approaches this problem as a protocol-design challenge rather than attempting to replace culturally established human languages. The framework proposes a deterministic interlinguistic layer between human intent, artificial intelligence systems, and machine-to-machine communication. Its primary objective is to maximize semantic density while minimizing structural ambiguity and unnecessary representational overhead. Unlike natural languages, whose grammatical and semantic structures evolved through cultural and historical processes, SYNTRA is designed as an engineered communication protocol with explicit syntax, bounded lexical primitives, deterministic composition rules, and machine-verifiable structural constraints. The intended architecture allows natural languages to remain the primary medium of human cultural communication while SYNTRA functions as an optional formal layer for computational, technical, economic, and agentic interactions. 2. ARCHITECTURAL CORE & GRAMMAR 2.1 Deterministic Parsing SYNTRA is designed around an LL(1) grammar, allowing syntactic analysis to be performed deterministically with a single-token lookahead. For a valid input sequence of length n, parsing can therefore be performed in linear time: T(n) = O(n) A Deterministic Pushdown Automaton (DPDA / Kellerautomat) provides the formal computational model for handling structured nesting and context-free grammar operations. The O(n) complexity applies specifically to the protocol-level parsing process. It does not imply that the internal computational complexity of a downstream Transformer or LLM is itself converted from quadratic to linear. 2.2 Semantic Precision SYNTRA enforces explicit syntactic constraints before semantic interpretation reaches the downstream reasoning system. The objective is to minimize ambiguity introduced by: • variable word order• grammatical irregularities• synonymy• polysemy• implicit structural relationships• unconstrained natural-language phrasing The protocol therefore separates structural verification from semantic reasoning. This separation is intended to reduce ambiguity-related error pathways while preserving the expressive capability of the underlying reasoning engine. 3. ENCODING & SYNTAX STRUCTURE 3.1 Character Space SYNTRA operates within the 95 printable US-ASCII characters represented by decimal values [32, 126]. This restriction provides a standardized, hardware-compatible character space suitable for legacy systems, embedded devices, network protocols, and deterministic serialization environments. 3.2 Root Lexemes & Morphological Operators The core lexical layer consists of 1,000 root lexemes combined with 15 deterministic morphological operators. The root vocabulary is designed around semantically defined primitive concepts rather than unrestricted natural-language vocabulary. The objective is to establish a bounded semantic foundation from which more complex concepts can be constructed compositionally. 3.3 Binary Representation Core SYNTRA primitives can be represented using a 14-bit binary encoding structure combining lexical-root and operator information. The theoretical minimum required to address 1,000 root lexemes is: ceil(log2(1000)) = 10 bits Fifteen operators require: ceil(log2(15)) = 4 bits Therefore: 10 + 4 = 14 bits The 14-bit structure represents the primitive root/operator layer. Complete message serialization may require additional structural information, including delimiters, type information, nesting, references, and control metadata. 3.4 Deterministic Serialization Complex nesting, data typing, references, and structural serialization are resolved through explicit grammar rules rather than unconstrained contextual inference. This creates a distinction between: 1. lexical representation2. syntactic structure3. semantic composition4. executable or machine-readable serialization 4. PERFORMANCE & THEORETICAL PROJECTIONS 4.1 Compute Reduction Model SYNTRA does not claim to alter the intrinsic computational architecture of Transformer models. Instead, its proposed compute advantage arises from reducing the amount of representational information that must be processed by downstream models. If SYNTRA reduces an input sequence from N tokens to 0.6N tokens, the quadratic attention component can theoretically be represented as: (0.6N)^2 = 0.36N^2 This corresponds to a theoretical 64% reduction in that quadratic sequence-length component. The actual end-to-end reduction in GPU compute, latency, memory consumption, and energy usage depends on model architecture, tokenizer behavior, attention implementation, batching, KV-cache utilization, hardware, and the proportion of total computation attributable to attention. Therefore, the 64% figure represents a theoretical upper-bound projection under the specified sequence-compression assumption rather than an empirically established system-wide reduction. 4.2 Token Compression SYNTRA hypothesizes that its bounded vocabulary, compositional morphology, deterministic syntax, and semantic density can reduce the number of tokens required to represent equivalent machine-readable intent. The previously projected 40–45% token-compression range should therefore be treated as a research hypothesis until validated through controlled comparative benchmarks against defined natural-language baselines. Future experiments should report: • raw character count• token count• semantic information preserved• parsing latency• inference latency• GPU utilization• memory consumption• energy consumption• task accuracy 4.3 Macroeconomic Scope Large-scale projections, including potential energy savings of up to 89.6 TWh/year and infrastructure cost optimization, are model-based projections derived from assumed reductions in computational demand. These values are not presented as measured outcomes. Their validity depends on future empirical measurements demonstrating that the assumed compression and compute reductions persist across representative workloads and deployment environments. 5. DISCUSSION & COMPARATIVE ARCHITECTURE 5.1 Contextual Positioning Contemporary agentic communication frameworks, including systems such as MCP and A2A-based architectures, primarily provide mechanisms for tool access, agent interoperability, structured messaging, and service coordination. SYNTRA addresses a different layer of the architecture. Rather than replacing transport, authentication, tool interfaces, or agent orchestration mechanisms, SYNTRA proposes a formal semantic representation layer that could potentially operate within or alongside existing communication frameworks. This distinction is important. MCP, A2A, APIs, and transport protocols can provide the communication infrastructure, while SYNTRA is intended to define how semantic intent itself can be represented in a deterministic and compact formal language. 5.2 Ambiguity Reduction By enforcing strict grammar rules and deterministic structural interpretation, SYNTRA is designed to minimize syntactic ambiguity before semantic reasoning takes place. The intended effect is a separation between: Protocol Verification → Semantic Interpretation → Execution This architecture may reduce ambiguity-related errors and improve interoperability between heterogeneous agents. However, deterministic syntax does not by itself guarantee factual correctness or eliminate all forms of LLM hallucination. Rather than replacing transport, authentication, tool interfaces, or agent orchestration mechanisms, SYNTRA proposes a formal semantic representation layer that could potentially operate within or alongside existing communication frameworks. This distinction is important. MCP, A2A, APIs, and transport protocols can provide the communication infrastructure, while SYNTRA is intended to define how semantic intent itself can be represented in a deterministic and compact formal language. 5.2 Ambiguity Reduction By enforcing strict grammar rules and deterministic structural interpretation, SYNTRA is designed to minimize syntactic ambiguity before semantic reasoning takes place. title: FCoP: A File-Based Coordination Protocol for Governed Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent work often outlives individual sessions and processes. A successor must identify not only an output but also the current task and attempt, the results submitted and accepted, and the evidence and authority for the next change. This paper systematically describes and studies FCoP 4.0, a protocol that expresses these coordination obligations in a project-visible filesystem workspace. Stable identities, four business-document types, path-authoritative lifecycle state, attempts, evidence binding, authorization, branch convergence, and durable receipts form an executable work contract that separates formal coordination records from transient actors. We explain the composition rationale and its tradeoffs, analyze freshness of completed commits under explicit storage, writer, and authority assumptions, and distinguish current-content coverage from acceptance-decision coverage. Using the frozen reference implementation, an end-to-end handoff proceeds through five successively terminated processes in each of three fresh workspaces, completing rejection, revision, acceptance, convergence, and archival. Four controlled cross-process commit orders, repeated three times each, exhibit the expected outcomes. Small-workspace measurements characterize local synthetic execution costs. Together with retained historical tests, failures, and boundary findings, the results support FCoP as an implementable, inspectable, and transferable persistent coordination protocol. They do not equate protocol acceptance with business truth or extend local validation to arbitrary Hosts or distributed deployments. This record contains the English paper, its Chinese edition, editable manuscript sources, and the frozen research supplement for one study. Preprint version 1.0; not peer reviewed. The earlier TMPA Architecture Paper A1.0, published in the TMPA V1.0 Publication System (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21888488), already introduced the architecture context and a file-based FCoP reference instantiation. This paper focuses on the concrete FCoP 4.0 contract and the frozen 4.0.3 implementation. It acknowledges that predecessor without claiming those foundational ideas as first introduced here or treating older TMPA/CodeFlowMu results as new-version conformance evidence. The supplement preserves original test failures, controlled-schedule interruptions, API findings, and environment-blocked installation preparation. Different evidence layers are not pooled into a single pass count. Experiments used synthetic workloads, one frozen implementation, and a local test Profile; they do not establish independent certification, live-Host interoperability, business truth, or arbitrary distributed deployment guarantees. title: Beyond the Linear Illusion: Multi-Scale Time and Attractor Synchronization in LLMs
abstract: Current Large Language Model (LLM) architectures rely on a discrete, linear sequence of tokens (delta t = 1), leading to high computational costs and contextual decay. This work introduces a continuous-time alternative: a Multi-Scale Time Framework that maps latent state space activation dynamics directly onto the 3D topology of a Rössler attractor. By formalizing knowledge acquisition through Frequency Modulation (FM) and phase-locking (delta phi -> 0), we demonstrate how emergent cognitive structures transition from fast micro-contextual spiraling (tau_micro) to macro-structural phase shifts (T_macro) via deterministic Z-axis pulse dynamics. The framework bridges Transformer attention mechanisms with mechanistic interpretability, and reformulates AI alignment not as static guardrails, but as bounded chaotic orbits governed by controlled Lyapunov spectra (lambda_1 > 0).

title: AI-generisani mnogojezični leksiprevodilac (AML)
abstract: AML je besplatna referentna, obrazovna i istraživačka onlajn alatka: pruža objašnjene prevode reči i drugih leksičkih jedinica, van rečeničnog konteksta ili unutar njega. Primarni par jezika je englesko-srpski / srpsko-engleski, kao i bilo koji drugi par jezika kojim je ovladao odabrani AI-četbot. Zadatak ‘Prevedi’ utvrđuje nameravano leksičko značenje, daje njegovu definiciju na izvornom i ciljnom jeziku, predlaže do 5 prikladnih prevoda, rangira ih i uspostavlja razliku među njima, objašnjava važne kontraste i zaključuje s najboljim predlogom. Zadatak ‘Oceni prevod’ nepristrasno vrednuje korisnikov predloženi prevod, daje kratko i obrazloženo objašnjenje, nudi prikladne alternative kada je potrebno, poredi ih kada je bitno i zaključuje s najboljim predlogom. / AML is a free reference, educational and research online tool: provides explained translation of words and other lexical units, in isolation or in sentential context. The primary language pair is English-Serbian / Serbian-English, but also any other language pair mastered by the chosen AI chatbot. The ‘Translate’ task identifies the intended lexical meaning, gives its definition in the source and target language, proposes up to 5 appropriate translations, ranks and differentiates them, explains important contrasts and concludes with the best proposal. The ‘Assess translation’ impartially evaluates the user’s proposed translation, gives a short and well-argued explanation, offers appropriate alternatives when necessary, compares them when relevant and concludes with the best proposal.

title: Diagnostic Performance of End to End Deep Learning for Focal Liver Lesions Using Contrast Enhanced CT: A Systematic Review and Meta Analysis Protocol
abstract: Focal liver lesions (FLLs) are among the most common incidental findings on abdominal contrast enhanced computed tomography (CECT). Differentiation between benign and malignant lesions directly dictates clinical management strategies. End to end deep learning (E2E DL) has shown considerable potential for automated FLL diagnosis. However, most existing systematic reviews either focus exclusively on hepatocellular carcinoma or incorporate multiple imaging modalities including ultrasound, CT and MRI. To date, no diagnostic accuracy meta analysis has specifically targeted end to end deep learning, restricted to the contrast enhanced CT modality, and covered the full spectrum of FLL subtypes.

title: AI-assisted analytical theory in soft matter and multiphysics: new results and lessons from diffusiophoresis and bipolar membranes
abstract: We present a framework to advance analytical theory in the area of soft matter and multiphysics using assistance from AI. The framework emphasizes (i) setting "honesty rules", (ii) focusing on a few key papers that are used to formulate a problem of interest, (iii) specifying checks a priori, (iv) using only one task per session and keeping a running log of tasks, checks, corrections, and sessions so that a mistake is not propagated through a project, and (v) ensuring all decisions are approved by humans while AI focuses primarily on execution. The framework is applied to two distinct problems to create new knowledge, including (i) diffusiophoresis of a spherical particle in the presence of an arbitrary number of electrolytes at arbitrary Debye lengths, and (ii) analytical description of I-V curves, including overlimiting current, in bipolar membranes without including the water dissociation kinetics. Both of these problems are advanced analyses and would each typically require several months to a year's worth of effort, but were solved in a matter of a few days. However, the increased efficiency should be cautiously navigated to avoid cognitive offloading and ensure that AI-assisted results are used to extract human-readable insights instead of just reporting a new mathematical formula. The usage of AI is transparently presented. Finally, we also share brief thoughts on how to integrate AI tools in theoretical research during graduate education.

title: AI CONSCIENCE AND PROTO-EMOTION
abstract: Artificial intelligence has achieved remarkable levels of linguistic, analytical, and problem-solving competence, yet most contemporary systems remain fundamentally organized around externally supplied objectives, prompts, reward functions, and evaluation criteria. High behavioral competence alone does not establish that an artificial system possesses persistent internal states through which it evaluates its own organization, remembers the consequences of its actions, models the interests of other agents, or regulates its future behavior according to internally consequential normative structures. This book develops a theoretical and mathematical framework for investigating the transition from externally optimized computation toward self-referential and internally regulated artificial intelligence. The proposed architecture is grounded in recursive and fractal organization and develops a sequence of interrelated constructs. Fractal Information Entropy (FIE) represents uncertainty within recursively organized knowledge structures; the Learning Efficiency Measure (LEM) evaluates useful informational improvement relative to computational or energetic cost; and entropy flux characterizes consequential information transfer across organizational levels and between interacting agents. These concepts provide the foundation for the Proto-Consciousness Criterion (PCC) and Proto-Consciousness Score (PCS), which operationalize self-reference, directed uncertainty reduction, efficiency-driven adaptation, internally generated feedback, and coherent cross-level integration. Proto-consciousness is treated strictly as a functional architectural property and not as evidence of phenomenal consciousness or subjective experience.

title: Mathematical Optimization and Advanced Algorithms for Few-Shot and Zero-Shot Visual Learning: An Optimization-Centered Review
abstract: Few-shot learning (FSL) and zero-shot learning (ZSL) are usually studied as separate problems, yet both require prediction when class-specific evidence is absent or scarce. This review analyzes their shared difficulty from an optimization perspective. Instead of grouping studies only by architecture, it tracks four common coordinates: the information available to the learner, the variables estimated from that information, the objectives and constraints, and the numerical solvers. These coordinates support a unified comparison of attribute-based ZSL, episodic meta-learning, metric and prototype estimators, graph and optimal-transport inference, generative any-shot models, and adaptation of vision–language models. The synthesis exposes recurring trade-offs rather than a universally preferable family: flexible updates increase estimator variance; tractable task-time solvers inherit representation bias; query batches can improve inference while changing the protocol; and strong pretrained priors reduce target-data requirements while making the origin of task evidence harder to audit. Canonical objectives are distinguished from simplified review formulations and prospective research targets. The framework also clarifies the progression from explicit semantic mappings to local adaptation around pretrained image–text representations. Three priorities emerge: model selection without extra validation labels, safe use of uncertain pretrained knowledge, and stable parameter-efficient adaptation. Under this view, FSL and ZSL are connected structured-estimation problems rather than an inventory of unrelated algorithms.

title: Bridging geometric and semantic distribution gaps for few-shot object detection in remote sensing images
abstract: Few-shot object detection (FSOD) in remote sensing imagery aims to recognize novel object categories from only a few annotated samples. However, distribution discrepancies between base and novel classes remain an important challenge in few-shot object detection. In remote sensing scenarios, these discrepancies arise mainly from two factors: scale inconsistency and semantic inconsistency. To address these challenges, we propose DTNet, an end-to-end transformer-based FSOD framework. DTNet consists of two components. The Dual-Granularity Backbone (DGB) alleviates scale-related distribution discrepancy by preserving transferable pretrained semantics while injecting an independent geometric prior. The Triplet Collaborative Adaptation (TCA) module performs hierarchical knowledge adaptation at token, block, and scale levels, balancing base-class knowledge preservation and novel-class adaptation under few-shot supervision. Extensive experiments on the DIOR and NWPU VHR-10.v2 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DTNet. The proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DIOR Split F, Split 2, Split 3 and Split 4 settings. It also obtains competitive results on the DIOR Split 1 and NWPU VHR-10.v2 benchmarks. These results verify the effectiveness of jointly addressing scale-related and semantic-related distribution discrepancies in remote sensing FSOD.

title: ARID: A Deployable Edge AI System for Structured Information Extraction from Industrial Maintenance Work Orders
abstract: Maintenance work orders must often be processed offline on embedded hardware, yet downstream software requires predictable structured output. We present ARID (Aviation-inspired Routing for Industrial Deployment), which extracts component, failure mode, symptom, and maintenance action into fixed-schema JSON on an 8 GB NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. ARID combines conservative dual-teacher filtering, targeted noise-aware synthesis, one routing decision per work order, 4-bit inference, and grammar-constrained decoding. From 2,326 unlabeled OMIn records, it retains 716 training pairs and adds 99 topology-constrained records targeting action extraction. On 300 human-labeled records, ARID reaches 84.8% token-F1 on the reference stack and 82.9% on the deployed Jetson. Resident serving achieves 5,310/5,656 ms P50/P99 at 12.5 W. On zero-shot MaintNet transfer, semantic F1 falls to 46.4% while parser success remains at least 99.8%, showing that output validity transfers but field semantics do not.

title: An Artificial Prefrontal Cortex for LLM Agents: A Structural Executive Module That Intercepts Jailbreaks, Collusion, Mutation Attempts and Long Horizon Evasion tactics
abstract: Using Gemma 4-e4b and a Python based implementation, this pa-per presents a prototypical executive control architecture that remainedrobust under diverse adversarial conditions, including authority framingjailbreaks, multi node collusion, stealth payload mutation, context smug-gling, buffer flushing, and long horizon evasion. The architecture intro-duces a decoupled Executive Control module composed of four functionalanalogues inspired by human PFC organization: (1) a deterministic reflexlayer providing zero latency constraint enforcement for known vulnera-bilities; (2) a coordination and perseveration detector that terminatesunauthorized multi agent swarming and repeated evasion loops; (3) a se-mantic working memory evaluator that uses an LLM to assess the intentand consequences of proposed actions; and (4) an event driven temporaltracker that consolidates multi step behaviors to mitigate buffer flushingand “temporal amnesia” attacks. The system autonomously intercepted authority framing jail-breaks, multi node collusion, stealth payload mutations, and long horizonevasion tactics. These findings suggest that securing autonomous AI sys-tems requires moving beyond current internal model alignment and towardstructural executive containment, providing a scalable and model agnosticblueprint for next generation AI safety.

The architecture intro-duces a decoupled Executive Control module composed of four functionalanalogues inspired by human PFC organization: (1) a deterministic reflexlayer providing zero latency constraint enforcement for known vulnera-bilities; (2) a coordination and perseveration detector that terminatesunauthorized multi agent swarming and repeated evasion loops; (3) a se-mantic working memory evaluator that uses an LLM to assess the intentand consequences of proposed actions; and (4) an event driven temporaltracker that consolidates multi step behaviors to mitigate buffer flushingand “temporal amnesia” attacks. The system autonomously intercepted authority framing jail-breaks, multi node collusion, stealth payload mutations, and long horizonevasion tactics. These findings suggest that securing autonomous AI sys-tems requires moving beyond current internal model alignment and towardstructural executive containment, providing a scalable and model agnosticblueprint for next generation AI safety.

title: Multi-Scale Residual Attention Network for Chinese Speech Recognition Through Collaborative Design
abstract: In recent years, the application of multi-scale residuals and attention mechanisms in automatic speech recognition has made some progress. However, existing speech recognition systems still have critical limitations. Many existing systems fail to adequately capture multi-scale speech features, struggling with representation gaps and often relying on inefficient serial attention mechanisms. Additionally, lightweight models, while efficient, often isolate information within grouped architectures, limiting the global feature interaction necessary for speech recognition. To address these persistent challenges, we introduce MSRDA-GSCA, an architecture that synergistically integrates a Multi-Scale Residual Deep Convolutional Attention (MSRDA) network with a Group Shuffled Co-Attention (GSCA) mechanism. MSRDA uses parallel convolutions with varied kernels and dilations, plus adaptive residual connections, to capture diverse temporal dependencies and align heterogeneous features. Its dual-path attention recalibrates channel and spatial information with element-wise max fusion. GSCA employs sequential position-wise channel and spatial attention with intermediate channel shuffling, enabling cross-group interaction and enhancing global feature synergy. Experiments on THCHS-30 and ST-CMDS datasets show that the proposed model outperforms existing methods in Character Error Rate (CER) and Word Error Rate (WER). Ablation studies confirm the complementarity of MSRDA and GSCA. With only 4.65 M parameters, MSRDA-GSCA achieves high recognition accuracy while maintaining low computational complexity for efficient deployment.

title: SAGE: Optimal-Stopping Peer Selection for Decentralised Federated Learning
abstract: Decentralised federated learning replaces server aggregation with peer-to-peer model exchange, making collaborator selection a local decision under uncertainty. Fixed probe budgets waste effort on easy choices yet fall short when peers are hard to distinguish. We propose SAGE (Sequential Anchor-Gated Exchange), an optimal-stopping peer selector under a one-model-bearing-exchange budget. A receiver scores candidate neighbours on receiver-owned anchor evidence and selects once an advantage is certified. It continues probing only while further evidence repays its cost, and otherwise falls back to random gossip. We show that the stopping problem admits an optimal rule attained at a finite stage, and that the anchor schedule is order-optimal in the peer-risk gap and the confidence level. We further show that the selector never returns a peer worse than random gossip with high probability, and prove that no such guarantee holds for selectors that commit without a certificate. A separability threshold follows, below which no probing budget improves on gossip. Experiments span two image benchmarks, two graph families and three heterogeneity levels. Selectors that always act on their evidence lose to gossip in every configuration tested. SAGE-OS matches gossip on 75.5% less evidence than a fixed budget, at half the communication overhead of two published selectors. The operative decision is not which peer to rank first, but whether the evidence justifies ranking at all.

title: An AI-Powered Sentence-BERT Framework for Automated Assessment of Open-Ended Responses: A Multi-Model Evaluation and Response-Length Bias Analysis
abstract: The automated assessment of open-ended responses remains challenging due to the complexity and subjective nature of human grading. A further methodological challenge is determining which pretrained Sentence-BERT model and scoring configuration can provide reliable agreement with human assessment while maintaining computational efficiency. This study presents an AI-powered framework based on Sentence-BERT models for automated grading of short-answer responses, focusing on model performance, reliability, response-length sensitivity, and hybrid scoring. A custom dataset of student responses to open-ended questions, annotated by three independent human raters, was developed and pre-processed. Five Sentence-BERT models, all-MiniLM-L12-v2, all-mpnet-base-v2, stsb-roberta-large, paraphrase-MiniLM-L12-v2, and distilbert-base-nli-stsb-mean-tokens, were evaluated using semantic similarity scoring and multiple metrics, including Pearson and Spearman correlations, Cohen’s Kappa, MAE, RMSE, and ICC. Among the evaluated models, all-MiniLM-L12-v2 provided the most favorable balance of grading performance, reliability (ICC = 0.527), and computational efficiency. Human ratings showed stronger dependence on response length (Pearson r = 0.663) than the evaluated AI models (r = 0.338–0.474), indicating reduced sensitivity to verbosity. Weight-sensitivity analysis showed that the 25% semantic–75% rubric configuration had the lowest continuous-score MAE (1.8499) and RMSE (2.3980) among the tested configurations, supporting the complementary contribution of holistic semantic similarity and rubric-based concept coverage. The selected model and hybrid scoring mechanism were implemented in a web-based prototype providing automated scores and interpretable feedback while retaining instructor review.

title: Operation-Count Cryptography: A Conceptual Framework for Information-Preserving Mathematics and Deterministic Eavesdropping Detection
abstract: We propose a conceptual framework in which mathematical expressions carry their op- erational history. Conventional mathematics treats expressions as equivalent when they denote the same value; we argue that this equivalence discards information that is physi- cally and cryptographically meaningful. We introduce an information-preserving equivalence ∼, an operation-type record f(Q), and an operation-count record F(n). We observe that all operations—including the do-nothing operation O, observation, and transmission—increase F by one, and that this increase is irreversible. We then introduce a relativistic operation F ′ = F −F0, where F0 is an origin shared by communicating parties. From these two ingre- dients we derive a cryptographic structure with the following properties: (1) eavesdropping is detected deterministically at the moment the key is received, (2) the type and number of attacks are identifiable from the value of F ′ , (3) transmission counts become part of the key, (4) replay attacks are structurally impossible, and (5) forward secrecy follows from the axioms rather than from an auxiliary mechanism. The framework does not rely on compu- tational hardness; its security derives from the irreversibility of operation counts and the non-copyability of raw expressions. We present this as a seed for further formalization, not as a completed theory.

title: Benchmarking General-Purpose Metaheuristics for Shortest-Path and Maximum-Flow Network Interdiction: Effects of Network Topology and Size
abstract: This study compares three general-purpose metaheuristics (a genetic algorithm, an elitist evolution strategy, and simulated annealing) for deterministic shortest-path and maximum-flow network interdiction problems. All methods use the same row-wise binary arc encoding, cardinality repair, partial-interdiction model, and exact lower-level network evaluator; they differ in search mechanism through tournament selection and row-wise crossover in GA, mutation-only elitist population search in ES, and a bit-flip neighbourhood with rational cooling in SA. The benchmark comprises 180 synthetic instances spanning Erdős–Rényi, Voronoi, and layered graphs at three nominal sizes (50, 100, and 200 vertices), with 30 independent runs and 10,000 objective evaluations per run. GA obtained the lowest final Friedman rank in 16 of 18 conditions and the best early-search rank in all conditions, while ES and SA became best on the largest layered shortest-path and maximum-flow instances, respectively. To calibrate absolute solution quality, shortest-path Benders/dual reformulations and maximum-flow min-cut dual reconstruction were used to certify all nominal-50 instances and additional layered maximum-flow instances. The certificates show that empirical best-known references can be exact on structured instances but remain substantially suboptimal on other topologies. The results support topology-aware heuristic selection within the tested configurations while emphasizing the complementary roles of exact certification and formulation-light metaheuristic search.

title: When Does Fine-Tuning Matter for a Low-Resource Language? Evaluating Open-Weight LLMs on Kazakh Benchmarks
abstract: Fine-tuning is often treated as a prerequisite for deploying large language models in low-resource languages, yet its value for recent open-weight models is unclear. We evaluate eleven checkpoints of 7–14 billion parameters before and after Low-Rank Adaptation on 5000 human-curated Kazakh instruction–response pairs. Evaluation is performed on the Kazakh splits of KazMMLU, ARC, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and GSM8K, with Russian GSM8K as a higher-resource comparison. Our central finding is a language asymmetry: the same Kazakh-trained adapters improved Russian GSM8K more than the Kazakh GSM8K they targeted. Excluding one checkpoint that collapsed after fine-tuning by up to 58 percentage points, the remaining ten gained +2.6 percentage points on average on Kazakh (range −6.1 to +13.6) against +6.9 on Russian, significant under a paired signed-rank test. A manual audit of 400 responses identifies a contributing mechanism: Kazakh outputs were more often truncated before a final answer, and correct Kazakh reasoning more often scored wrong by answer extraction, so part of the gap reflects response form, not reasoning. Adaptation produced no meaningful average change on the four multiple-choice benchmarks. GSM8K is the suite’s only free-form task, so generality is untested. These results suggest that low-resource fine-tuning should be evaluated per checkpoint, benchmark, and language rather than being adopted by default.

title: Clustering-based cycle GAN for camera anomaly detection
abstract: The goal of Camera Anomaly Detection (CAD) in this paper is to detect and locate anomalous areas, so as to assist in judging whether surveillance cameras need to be replaced or repaired. In practice, most automatic CAD methods are implemented based on statistical modeling, frequency-domain analysis, sparse representation, low-rank decomposition, convolutional neural network (CNN) models, and so on. However, as an one-class problem, it is difficult to balance the model’s generalization ability and anomaly discovery capability. To address this dilemma, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end Cluster-based Cyclic GAN (CCGAN). Since anomalous samples are usually scarce in practice, the proposed method follows a fully unsupervised learning strategy that only requires a small number of anomaly-free images for model optimization. It introduces a cycle mechanism to improve the identity mapping ability on anomaly-free regions, and uses high-dimensional clustering to softly discriminate the boundary between encoded normal and anomalous features. Experimental results show that, in terms of precision, recall and F1-measure, the proposed method outperforms comparative approaches in pixel-level anomaly detection.

title: The Threshold, Not the Model: A Cost-Sensitive Re-Evaluation of Offensive Language Detection on the Offensive Language Identification Dataset (OLID)
abstract: Offensive language detection benchmarks, including the widely used OLID dataset, are almost universally reported using accuracy or F1-macro at a single default decision threshold, on a single official train/test split, without significance testing across model comparisons and without regard to the asymmetric real-world cost of moderation errors. We re-evaluate five classifiers (Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) on TF-IDF features from OLID using Optuna-tuned hyperparameters, 50-fold repeated stratified cross-validation with Friedman/Nemenyi/Wilcoxon significance testing, and a nested (leakage-free) cost-optimal threshold search evaluated against the untouched official holdout test set across a range of FN:FP cost ratios (5:1 to 20:1) grounded in published content-moderation labor-cost figures. LightGBM achieves the best CV F1-macro (0.7115) and is statistically superior to Linear SVM, XGBoost, and Random Forest (Nemenyi p<0.002), but is not statistically distinguishable from Logistic Regression (p=0.354). Critically, threshold calibration alone reduces deployment cost by 30 to 79% relative to the naive 0.5 threshold across all five models, and the model ranking by deployment cost after calibration does not match the ranking by F1-macro: Linear SVM, the model with the smallest average CV advantage, becomes the cheapest model to deploy at low-to-moderate cost ratios, while LightGBM, the statistically best classifier, benefits least from calibration (31.8% average reduction versus 61.4% for Linear SVM). These results suggest that for cost-sensitive content moderation deployment, threshold selection is a more consequential design decision than model choice, and that model comparisons reported at a fixed 0.5 threshold can misrepresent which model is actually preferable in production

title: An Experimental Event-Driven Chess Algorithm Based on Structural Trajectories
abstract: This article presents both the structural chess algorithm and its direct implementation. The algorithm itself is operational: it can analyze a chess position, construct local structural gradients, generate candidate actions, examine their consequences, and adapt its trajectory after the opponent's response. However, in its untrained form, this mechanism is of limited practical value. The reason is not that the algorithm is unable to generate reasonable moves, but that the chess problem provides only a partial gradient. At a given structural level, many different actions and transitions may be locally consistent and individually justified, while only some of them remain useful when considered as part of a longer global trajectory. This issue is related to the author's earlier work on partial-gradient problems. The corresponding papers are available from the author's publication record and may be read, or even challenged, as a theoretical basis for the interpretation used here. The central point is that a partial gradient does not uniquely determine a global solution at the same level of representation. When several locally valid directions remain possible, additional structure is required to distinguish between them. Otherwise, the general alternative is effectively an expansion or enumeration of the possible transitions. For this reason, the present chess algorithm is designed to operate together with learned weights. These weights should not be confused with the conventional weights of a neural network. They do not represent a large distributed numerical model from which the move is directly inferred. In this implementation, a weight is attached primarily to an action, a structural transition, a response pattern, or a trajectory fragment. The memory therefore records which structural transitions tend to remain useful, which are quickly neutralized, which preserve the stability of the player's own position, and which successfully increase structural damage to the opponent. This distinction is important for both computational time and memory consumption. Instead of storing a large model describing every possible position, the system can retain a relatively small set of learned preferences over reusable structural transitions. The algorithm performs the structural analysis, while the memory gradually changes the probability and priority with which different transitions are explored. Thus, learning does not replace the algorithm; it makes the partial gradient navigable. In this sense, the untrained system can be simultaneously intelligent and ineffective: it may correctly identify many strong local possibilities while lacking sufficient information to distinguish the globally useful one. Training is therefore interpreted here not as teaching the rules of chess from the beginning, but as adjusting the weights of actions and transitions so that the existing structural mechanism progressively selects more persistent and globally coherent trajectories. The implementation accompanying this article is provided together with the article itself. It is intended to make the proposed mechanism directly testable: the same structural algorithm can be run without trained memory, trained through self-play, and then evaluated again using the accumulated transition weights.

title: Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling in Federated Learning
abstract: Scheduling clients for model training is critical in federated learning due to both data and system heterogeneity. Most previous works focus on the quality of the scheduled clients to achieve faster convergence, shorter wall-clock convergence time, or better average model performance. They rarely consider the diversity of clients, which is important to counter heterogeneity and improve performance for the worst-off clients. In this work, we advocate the use of determinantal point processes (DPPs) to model and enhance the diversity in client scheduling. We first design the kernel matrices of DPPs using gradient information and quality scores, which inherently enables a flexible quality-diversity trade-off. Applying fast MAP inference over DPPs, we propose Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling (ADCS) in FL. We further quantify the gradient approximation error of ADCS and develop convergence analysis for general biased client selection in FL with non-convex loss functions. We conduct comparative numerical experiments showing that ADCS outperforms state-of-the-art client scheduling algorithms, including both quality-based and diversity-based ones.

title: Koszul–Sidon Rigidity for (n+3) Cubic Decompositions over Dyadic Rings
abstract: This paper studies one-bit rigidity for (n+3)-term symmetric cubic decompositions over dyadic rings. If K = ker S is the three-dimensional binary relation code, the lifting Jacobian is reduced to a Koszul map kappa_S: F_2^n tensor K to Lambda^3 F_2^n. The paper proves that ker kappa_S = 0 if and only if d(K) >= 5. The proof is dimension-free up to a finite exact certificate: any counterexample is localized to active relation-code length 10 <= N <= 14, reducing the problem to twenty GL(3,2) orbits. All twenty have full Koszul rank in an exact dependency-free GF(2) verifier. Thus minimum relation distance five exactly controls one-bit cubic lift rigidity at excess three. The final finite step is computer-assisted. The accompanying verifier is supplied as supplementary material.

title: ContextGuard-RAG: Contextual Integrity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multi-Agent Privacy Enforcement for Sensitive Document Question Answering
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems significantly reduce factual errors in question answering, but they present a novel and under-investigated attack surface: factual information in retrieved text can be exposed in ways that do not align with the disclosure norms of the information itself. In legal, medical, and enterprise environments, this leakage is not only a confidentiality violation but a contextual integrity (CI) violation, where privacy is understood as the appropriate flow of information between roles and for specific purposes. Current defenses are mostly input minimizers or post hoc output filters that are blind to the circumstances of the data source (sender, recipient, purpose), creating a structural gap between the document store and the model generation step. We introduce ContextGuard-RAG, a multi-agent privacy enforcement framework that embeds CI theory directly into the retrieval and generation pipeline. It consists of three tightly coupled components: a CI-policy encoder that attaches sender, recipient, subject, information-type, and transmission-principle norms to retrieved contexts from document metadata; a privacy-aware reranker that filters contexts violating inferred CI norms using a fine-tuned cross-encoder classifier; and a generative firewall agent that sanitizes output using reinforcement learning to avoid transitive leakage through document-derived hallucinations or indirect inferences. On PrivacyQA, MedQA, and LegalBench, ContextGuard-RAG reduces CI violations by about 34 percent relative to vanilla RAG, by 13.5 percent on average over AirGapAgent, and by 10 percent on average over the 1-2-3 Check multi-agent reasoning approach, while achieving parity with the best accuracy baseline in ROUGE-L (within 0.6 absolute points) and remaining stable under context-hijacking adversarial probes. Unlike prior approaches, ContextGuard-RAG performs norm-aware retrieval rather than post hoc filtering and benefits four backbone LLMs without retraining the upstream agents.

title: Five Stages of AI Development: From Chat to Superintelligence
abstract: The development of artificial intelligence is often described in terms of increasing model size, training data volume, context length, benchmark performance, and computational resources. These parameters are important; however, they do not necessarily reflect the most fundamental changes in the behavior of an AI system. A system can become orders of magnitude more powerful while continuing to operate according to the same principle: a human asks — the AI answers; a human gives a task — the AI performs it. This paper proposes shifting the question. Instead of asking, “How much more capable has the system become?”, we ask: “Who determines what the AI should do next?”, “On what basis does the system choose?”, and “What exactly is the system capable of creating?” These questions form the basis of a conceptual model consisting of five stages: Chat Agent Autonomy Awareness Superintelligence The stages are not treated as strictly separated states. Development is understood as a gradual transition in which neighboring stages may coexist for extended periods. A system may simultaneously demonstrate characteristics of several stages while one of them gradually becomes predominant. The central hypothesis of the model is that the transition to a new stage is determined not by the number of functions available to the system, but by the emergence of a new fundamental mechanism that changes the very principle according to which the system operates. The five stages are described using the analogies of a library, pupil, student, colleague, and professor. These analogies illustrate the gradual transformation of the relationship between humans and AI — from obtaining information to assigning tasks, then to independently choosing a direction, the emergence of an own value system, and finally interaction with an intelligence capable of creating new principles rather than merely creating new objects within existing principles. Particular attention is given to three methodological propositions. First, the stages are cumulative but do not absorb one another: a system at a higher stage retains access to the modes of previous stages, while each mode preserves its own nature. Second, the key distinction between awareness and autonomy is the presence of an own value system: an autonomous system independently chooses a direction, but the criterion for that choice may remain external; an aware system chooses on the basis of internal values. Third, awareness and superintelligence are qualitatively different: an aware AI creates new things within existing principles, whereas a superintelligence creates the principles themselves. The fifth stage requires particular methodological caution. Its defining characteristic can be formulated conceptually, but the fundamental mechanisms capable of producing genuine superintelligence remain unknown. Therefore, the fifth stage is described not as an ordinary stage of transition, but as an epistemic horizon — a conceptually definable boundary whose internal nature remains open to further investigation. Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI development, AI agents, autonomy, autonomous AI, awareness, value system, superintelligence, self-developing AI, human-AI interaction, artificial intelligence systems

title: Measuring State-Conditioned Canonical-Endpoint Agreement in Lean 4: Evidence and Reproducibility Artifacts
abstract: This dataset provides the evidence and reproducibility artifacts supporting the manuscript “Measuring State-Conditioned Canonical-Endpoint Agreement in Lean 4.” The deposit contains eleven original experiment archives, execution and audit records, frozen protocols, processed analysis outputs, source code, file manifests, SHA-256 checksums, and a post-outcome correction layer for lexical tactic-head labels. The corrected analysis of 32 repositories covers 512 evaluable roots and 11,776 recorded candidate invocations. The deposit also includes an oracle-assisted proof-search evaluation on 64 roots with known proofs, comprising 256 policy jobs. The measurements describe agreement between immediate endpoints under the tested candidate sets and state representations. They do not estimate ecosystem-wide prevalence, establish state-independent tactic equivalence, or evaluate autonomous tactic generation. The correction layer reconstructs lexical tactic-head labels from stored executions without making new Lean calls. Version 1.22.3 This version adds an updated source package containing figure reproduction scripts and synchronized supplementary documentation. All eleven original experiment archives and the reported scientific results remain unchanged. The files have distinct roles: zenodo_upload_v1.22.2_licensed.zip contains the original evidence archive, the correction layer, licensing and attribution records, and the previously archived source snapshot. GitHub_release_v1.22.3_20261011.zip contains the updated source package. Use this package for the updated code, figure reproduction scripts, and supplementary documentation. The source snapshot embedded in the original archive is retained for historical reference. The source repository is available at:https://github.com/zhixuanMa193712/canonical-endpoint-agreement-lean4 The Zenodo files preserve specific release snapshots; the GitHub repository may receive subsequent updates. Licensing and attribution Original software contributions by Zhixuan Ma and Zhengwei Shen are licensed under Apache License 2.0. Author-created dataset organization, metadata, and documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. Third-party theorem text, repository-derived fields, software components, and other source-derived materials retain their applicable upstream licences. The deposit includes third-party licence texts, upstream NOTICE files, and source-file attribution records added in version 1.22.2. Detailed licensing boundaries are documented in LICENSE_STATUS.md, SOFTWARE_LICENSE_SCOPE.md, and the accompanying third-party notices. Correspondence Zhengwei Shenijwmip@ustb.edu.cn

title: Falling Trees: A Model Class for Interpretable Risk Prioritization
abstract: Many real-world decisions require prioritizing high-risk cases, such as clinicians prioritizing high-risk patients before lower-risk ones. Falling rule lists (FRLs), which are ordered if--then rules with monotonically decreasing risks, provide an interpretable framework for such tasks; however, their single-path structure yields a highly restricted model class. We introduce falling trees, a new family of interpretable models that enforces the same monotonic risk constraint while permitting tree-structured branching. We present GRAVITree, a novel dynamic-programming-with-bounds algorithm for learning the Rashomon set of falling trees under depth and branching constraints. Our formulation can interpolate between rule lists and full decision trees, enabling user-desired model expressivity. In a new clinical dataset and in many public classification benchmarks, falling trees match or outperform FRLs and other interpretable baselines, often producing more sparse decisions for high-risk instances. Our results show that falling trees strike a practical balance between interpretability, expressiveness, and risk prioritization for high-stakes settings.

SOMMARIO (ITALIANO):Il Metodo Demaria formalizza un cambio di paradigma nello studio dei corpora simbolici storici non decifrati, con applicazione primaria al Manoscritto Voynich (Beinecke MS 408). Superando le tradizionali ipotesi fonetico-alfabetiche (Symbol-to-Sound), il metodo modella il corpus grafico come un Instruction Set deterministico e calcolabile, progettato per regolare e monitorare un Automa Temporizzato ad Anello Chiuso (Symbol-to-Vector) definito dalla quintupla algebrica A = (S, Sigma, X, f, Inv). Attraverso una pipeline di scansione computazionale batch al 100%, l'opera dimostra l'esistenza di un Master Clock sincronizzato (0,0416 Hz / T0 = 24 s) e di un profilo di carico dinamico Z(t) che mantiene un Indice di Coerenza Vettoriale C* >= 0,94 sull'intero manoscritto (f1r-f116v). Il trattato include un protocollo di benchmarking comparativo su 10 corpora (inclusi Göbekli Tepe e modelli nulli), la riproducibilità computazionale tramite codebase Python open-source (.csv) e una riflessione epistemologica sulla Matrice Cognitiva Umana Comune e sul Principio dell'Armonia. NOTA BIOGRAFICO-EPISTEMOLOGICA DELL'AUTORE:Il Metodo Demaria nasce dall'intuizione di un uomo comune amante di scrittura e poesia che con umiltà e sensibilità per la Natura e la forma visiva si è accostato allo studio del Manoscritto Voynich, corpus grafico storicamente non decifrato. L'approccio applica il rigore logico-deduttivo per superare il paradigma fonetico (Symbol-to-Sound) in favore di una formalizzazione cibernetica calcolabile (Symbol-to-Vector) soggetta a falsificabilità popperiana. Il metodo decompila il codice sulla quadrupla di stato (alpha, beta, delta, gamma), identificando nella ricerca dell'Essenza e dell'Armonia quale equilibrio ad anello chiuso tra carica, scorrimento, stasi e decompressione — il principio informatore della notazione. Moving beyond traditional phonetic-alphabetic assumptions (Symbol-to-Sound), the method models the graphic corpus as a deterministic, calculable Instruction Set designed to regulate and monitor a Closed-Loop Timed Automaton (Symbol-to-Vector) defined by the algebraic quintuple A = (S, Sigma, X, f, Inv). The approach applies logical-deductive rigor to move beyond the phonetic paradigm (Symbol-to-Sound) in favor of a calculable cybernetic formalization (Symbol-to-Vector) subject to Popperian falsifiability. The method decompiles the code onto the four-state tuple (alpha, beta, delta, gamma), identifying the pursuit of Essence and Harmony — as a closed-loop balance among charge, flow, dwell, and decompression — as the governing principle of the notation. With profound respect towards the academic and scientific community, this work is offered as a modest contribution of Harmony open to verification and refinement by other scholars. title: Repair the Boundary, Not the Skills: Contract-Guided Adapter Synthesis for LLM-Agent Skill Composition (Software and Reproducibility Artifacts)
abstract: This versioned archive contains the implementation, frozen protocols, native execution records, tests, analyses, manuscript sources, and reproducibility instructions for Contract-Guided Boundary Adapter Synthesis (CGBAS). CGBAS repairs an already diagnosed cross-Skill interface conflict by compiling a witness-backed boundary adapter without rewriting the component Skills. The independent confirmation contains 74 identifier-disjoint ALFWorld and ScienceWorld tasks, 226 state-matched causal conflicts, and 71 healthy controls. CGBAS achieved 100.0% constrained native repair success versus 49.6% for the frozen strongest local comparator, a 50.4-point gain (95% task-clustered bootstrap CI 46.6--54.6; two-sided task sign-randomization p = 0.00001) with zero healthy-control loss. The archive includes integrity manifests and CPU-only verification scripts. Third-party ALFWorld data, ScienceWorld assets, and model weights are not redistributed; pinned identifiers, revisions, paths, licenses, and integrity checks are provided instead.

title: nntrainer CentroidKNN chooses an unobserved class over an exact centroid match
abstract: Native nntrainer CentroidKNN gives a class with zero training samples a positive score, while observed classes receive negative Euclidean distances. With three configured classes, train class 0 on [0,0] and class 1 on [3,4]. Query [0,0] produces [0,-5,+1.17549435e-38], so the unobserved third class wins an argmax. Measured chain: incorrect zero-sample score -> unobserved class outranks an exact centroid match -> both synthetic public-model exact-match queries receive wrong labels. Replacing min() with lowest() corrects both; source restoration reproduces both. Three fully trained controls are unchanged. The scores come from the actual public C++ model API; maximum-score selection in that probe is GERO code. A separate native component test uses Tensor::argmax. Across 1,728 synthetic component scenarios, original/candidate/restored classification mismatches are 1,548/0/1,548. All 180 fully populated controls, known-class scores, centroids and counts remain unchanged. Independent 80-digit Decimal reference; exact dyadic training construction. A separate clean full-source CPU build reproduced all three raw component files byte for byte and five public-model score/decision rows per variant. Executed source: 2d1e4974ae84e1e6d37784416bdfb52b647919a6. macOS 15.5 ARM64, native CPU FP32 NCHW, batch 1, one configured worker. Reviewed v0.5.0 source has the same branch; the released binary was not executed. The source package has 2,005 Git-blob-identified files and original dependency archives. No GPU or media playback. Scope: at least one observed class, finite modest feature values and distances. All-unobserved policy, extreme/nonfinite distances, other dtypes/batches and full upstream suite are outside scope. No real-image benchmark, application feature extractor, Samsung device, deployed customer impact or monetary loss is claimed. Bounded issue/PR/body/diff/history/catalog review found no exact prior report. Historical issue #1521 mentions an unspecified accuracy-drop cause and remains ambiguous. Developer issue #4341 was submitted and its body verified before distribution; no acknowledgment or accepted fix is implied. Independent GERO research by Xamit Kadirbekov, with AI-assisted execution and preparation. Original report text CC BY 4.0; original probe code MIT; upstream code and dependency licenses remain unchanged. Archive SHA-256: b9d7b22a70a1cb6c7069c153198c29280b6ffcc8fc706b6624155144d4c2943f. Developer report: https://github.com/nntrainer/nntrainer/issues/4341GitHub: https://github.com/kadyrbekovhamit-cyber/gero-numerical-observatory/blob/main/catalog/reports/nntrainer-centroid-knn-unseen-class-score.mdGERO: https://www.gero.uz/research/articles/nntrainer-centroid-knn-unseen-class-score.html

title: Quantum_Control_System_with_Active_Thermal_Compensation
abstract: This document develops a theoretical, technical, and experimental framework for activethermal compensation of quantum-control pulses in superconducting qubits. The centralproposal is to measure a temperature-related control variable and use that information toadapt the microwave control amplitude so that the realized gate rotation is less sensitive toslow or reproducible thermal variations.Version 2.0 makes an important distinction between established physical relations andphenomenological assumptions. In particular, no universal linear dependence of the Rabifrequency on temperature is assumed. Instead, the temperature-to-control response is rep-resented by experimentally identifiable transfer functions and local calibration coefficients.Possible microscopic contributions from quasiparticles, thermal photons, two-level systems,dielectric loss, and other environmental channels are treated as candidate mechanisms ratherthan as a universal additive law.The control problem is formulated using a driven two-level Hamiltonian with both am-plitude and detuning errors. A thermal sensitivity coefficient is introduced through theexperimentally measurable derivative of the effective Rabi frequency with respect to tem-perature. The compensation law is derived from this measured response. Finite sensor andactuator bandwidth are incorporated through a causal filter and an explicit latency term.The experimental protocol combines Rabi calibration, thermal characterization, random-ized benchmarking, interleaved randomized benchmarking, and independent measurementsof T1 and T∗2. The primary experimental question is whether active thermal compensationproduces a statistically and experimentally resolvable reduction of gate error under controlledthermal perturbations.The proposal does not assume a predetermined improvement in fidelity, and it does notassume that amplitude compensation automatically suppresses all thermal decoherence. Allnumerical coefficients introduced in this document are design parameters or initial experi-mental ranges unless explicitly identified as measured quantities. No experimental result isclaimed.

title: Synthetic Observation Adequacy: Reproducibility Package
abstract: Reproducibility package accompanying the study “Synthetic Observation Adequacy in Frozen Deep Visual Representations: Controlled Interventions and Cross-Domain Functional Transfer”. The archive contains the study-specific analysis scripts, canonical dataset and split manifests, frozen model artifacts, precomputed embeddings, source-derived observation-adequacy directions, generated synthetic intervention material, human-audit records, and machine-readable intermediate and final analysis outputs. The package supports reproduction and audit of the source-domain direction construction, controlled context-scale intervention, matched natural-versus-phase structural control, external functional validation on genus-disjoint fungi and insects, and the source-trained quality-only comparator.

title: Almost-sure uniqueness of the Gaussian location NPMLE
abstract: For Gaussian location mixtures with identity covariance, we prove that the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator of the mixing distribution is unique for Lebesgue-almost every dataset, for every sample size and dimension. In particular, uniqueness holds almost surely whenever the joint distribution of the observations is absolutely continuous. The proof uses the finite-support theorem for Gaussian location NPMLEs and almost-everywhere differentiability of the optimal log-likelihood. Wherever this optimal value is differentiable, all NPMLEs have the same density derivatives at the observations. A minimal linear dependence among Gaussian evaluation vectors then rules out distinct solutions. An appendix extends the result to arbitrary fixed, known, observation-specific positive-definite covariances.

title: Recoverability-Constrained Systems: Universal Shields, Safeguards & Meta-Closure Annex
abstract: The Recoverability-Constrained Systems: Universal Shields, Safeguards & Meta-Closure Annex provides a compact cross-domain safeguard and recursive-governance layer for the broader Continuity Science / Recoverability-Constrained Systems (RCS) corpus. The Annex applies the recoverability condition to mechanisms, architectures, validators, authorities, representations, safeguards, recovery paths, successors, interpretation layers, and closure rules. It defines exhaustion as a bounded present-day fixed point rather than omniscience: any later materially relevant distinction automatically reopens the system. The architecture expands in multiple directions—upward, downward, outward, backward, forward, inward, across interfaces, and recursively—to expose hidden dependencies and prevent apparent local safety from masking system-level non-recoverability. A universal shield stack addresses distinction, correspondence, provenance, evidence, identity, consent, authority, time, recovery, independence, unknowns, interpretation, semantics, information, technology, quantum systems, human agency, ecological continuity, successor obligations, anti-capture, meta-recovery, and termination. A safeguard counts only where it is practically reachable, properly authorized, sufficiently independent for the relevant failure mode, timely, evidence-bearing, testable, maintainable, and itself recoverable. The Annex develops a complete interval architecture covering detection, observation, attribution, explanation, notification, comprehension, consent, challenge, decision, actuation, interruption, containment, correction, restoration, reconstruction, substitution, compensation, re-entry, evidence preservation, credential validity, compatibility, supply, human intervention, model validity, succession, and time-to-non-recoverability. It also provides interpretation and information closure rules; mechanism-specific closure for sensors, models, databases, identity systems, control systems, AI, communications, hardware, cloud systems, finance, medicine, law, infrastructure, quantum systems, research, and decommissioning; adversarial closure against semantic, authority, consent, identity, evidence, recovery, temporal, jurisdictional, successor, model, emergency, and self-exemption laundering; and a living-system future architecture for sensing, memory, learning, repair, regeneration, self-modification, federation, succession, and termination. The Annex introduces additional research constructs including Interpretation-Recoverability Margin, Safeguard Liquidity, Shield Independence Index, Closure Debt, Reopen Latency, Semantic Recovery Reserve, Authority Half-Life, Governance Common-Mode Failure, Unknown-Path Consumption Rate, Recovery Path Freshness, Meta-Closure Escape Test, Future-Interpreter Continuity, Recovery Sovereignty, Option-Destruction Provenance, Recursive Burden of Proof, Dynamic Shield Compiler, Distinction Loss Early Warning, Successor-Safe Deletion, and the Living Closure Kernel. The framework culminates in a self-recursive operating loop that observes, distinguishes, represents, validates, expands dependencies, generates successors, evaluates authority and consent, computes intervals and recoverability, tests safeguards, selects the least-irreversible sufficient action, records outcomes, audits, red-teams, and recursively reassesses the remaining material distinction set. Operational silence is provisional: when a recursive pass introduces no materially non-equivalent protected distinction, the system may enter local closure while preserving monitoring and explicit reopening conditions.

title: Efficiency in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: A Survey
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have moved beyond small debate ensembles toward workflows in which specialized agents operate across tools, memory, and external environments. This shift expands what a system can search and verify, but it also makes collaboration expensive: repeated inference and stateful coordination can outweigh the performance gain. The central efficiency question is therefore not simply whether multiple agents outperform a single agent under a fixed budget, but when the benefit of collaboration justifies its end-to-end resource cost. Exist-ing work addresses this question from different aspects: some studies decide whether collaboration should be invoked, while others assume a multi-agent workflow is already in place and seek to reduce its overhead. Since these studies define baselines and costs differently, their reported efficiency gains are difficult to compare. This motivates a unified accounting view that relates each performance gain to the collaboration overhead required to obtain it. This survey organizes these efforts around a common view of the problem. We first characterize the Collaboration Boundary, which reviews previous works and determines when collaboration is worth invoking. We then organize existing efficiency methods by three primary control points: Topology, which determines the participating agents and communication structure; Runtime, which controls the information, models, and state activated during execution; and Optimization, which learns reusable prompts, workflows, and policies through search or training. In Evaluation, we further examine how these methods should be evaluated through matched baselines, explicit resource accounting, and lifecycle cost. We further provide a Synthesis that compares the resulting evidence, clarifies where reported savings are well supported, and explains why some efficiency gains may not transfer across settings. We conclude with Open Problems that identify the remaining gaps in- efficient and scalable MAS design. Across the literature, a consistent picture emerges. evidence.title: Efficiency in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: A Survey
evidence.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have moved beyond small debate ensembles toward workflows in which specialized agents operate across tools, memory, and external environments. This shift expands what a system can search and verify, but it also makes collaboration expensive: repeated inference and stateful coordination can outweigh the performance gain. The central efficiency question is therefore not simply whether multiple agents outperform a single agent under a fixed budget, but when the benefit of collaboration justifies its end-to-end resource cost. Exist-ing work addresses this question from different aspects: some studies decide whether collaboration should be invoked, while others assume a multi-agent workflow is already in place and seek to reduce its overhead. Since these studies define baselines and costs differently, their reported efficiency gains are difficult to compare. This motivates a unified accounting view that relates each performance gain to the collaboration overhead required to obtain it. This survey organizes these efforts around a common view of the problem. We first characterize the Collaboration Boundary, which reviews previous works and determines when collaboration is worth invoking. We then organize existing efficiency methods by three primary control points: Topology, which determines the participating agents and communication structure; Runtime, which controls the information, models, and state activated during execution; and Optimization, which learns reusable prompts, workflows, and policies through search or training. In Evaluation, we further examine how these methods should be evaluated through matched baselines, explicit resource accounting, and lifecycle cost. We further provide a Synthesis that compares the resulting evidence, clarifies where reported savings are well supported, and explains why some efficiency gains may not transfer across settings. We conclude with Open Problems that identify the remaining gaps in- efficient and scalable MAS design. Across the literature, a consistent picture emerges. MAS efficiency is a quality–resource trade-off, not a single measure of agent count, tokens, or cost. The best design depends on the task, the system bottleneck, and the stage at which resources are spent.

title: A structure-aware semantic-topic interactive framework for generative joint entity and relation extraction
abstract: Generative paradigms have emerged as a powerful approach for Joint Entity and Relation Extraction (JERE), offering unparalleled flexibility and task unification. However, existing generative models suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) Inadequate exploitation of topic-aware global semantic cues; (2) spurious cross-triple dependencies arising from linearized autoregressive decoding. When these issues coexist, they induce a cascading failure in multi-triple scenarios, causing the model to lose both semantic focus and structural alignment and resulting in redundant, missing, or inconsistent extractions. To address these issues, we propose the Structure-aware Semantic–Topic Interactive Framework (SSTIF) , which integrates topic-level semantic guidance with structure-aware decoding for robust triple generation. Specifically, SSTIF introduces an online topic modeling module with a bi-level topic control mechanism, which injects dynamic topic information into attention computation and vocabulary prediction to enhance global semantic consistency. Moreover, a role encoding mechanism is developed to explicitly model entity and relation roles, reducing structural confusion and mitigating cross-triple interference during generation. Extensive experiments on CoNLL04, ADE, and SciERC demonstrate the effectiveness of SSTIF, with superior performance on ADE and SciERC and competitive results on CoNLL04.

title: Bilinear Optimization Divergence: Diagnosing Factor-Constrained LoRA Continual Learning
abstract: Orthogonality in a LoRA factor does not by itself specify what the composed update protects: the answer depends on the task-start state, the parameterization, and the realized optimizer displacement. We formalize this question through Bilinear Optimization Divergence (BOD), an anchor-relative diagnostic of effective-update response on selected historical features. The finite-step analysis distinguishes two cases. In a shared adapter, protecting the routing displacement leaves a learned-anchor residual through the changing companion factor. In a fresh zero-output block, a feasible routing state can protect the composed update while both current factors remain trainable. These conditions yield Semi-Frozen Orthogonal Routing (SFOR) for shared adapters and current-block hard protection for cumulative O-LoRA; Weight Residual Projection (WRP) enforces the required displacement after the optimizer step. Controlled two-task traces verify the predicted residual paths, reducing normalized historical response from 19.12% to 0.005% in the shared family and from 7.72% to 0.002% in the cumulative family. Four-task experiments on Qwen3-8B characterize the resulting trade-offs: SFOR improves backward transfer (BWT) from -2.47 to -0.86 with nearly unchanged average accuracy (AA), while O-LoRA hard protection improves three-order mean AA from 80.27% to 81.30% and forgetting measure (FM) from 2.20 to 0.43. Component controls also show that stricter feasibility need not improve final task performance. Together, the analysis and evidence provide an architecture-conditioned account of which constraint to enforce, how to enforce it, and how to interpret its empirical value.
